arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL DATE, AND THE RECORD HAD NONE AT ALL. The recovered v4 research places William H. Adams on an 1835 Chicago poll list; it does not say when the poll was taken, and nothing in the corpus says when he came. The only thing the evidence bears is that he was in Chicago at some point during 1835, so the value carried here is the last day that evidence can reach, at 'not_later_than' precision — the same shape the town's letter-list arrivals take, and a bound rather than a date. Whether he was standing here on 1 July 1835 is the open question present_on_scene_date records as uncertain. The block arrived from PR #670 with a null value and no precision, which the gate could not read.

persons.note: RECOVERED CONFIRMED RESIDENT. The v4 census/resident research classifies William H. Adams as A — CONFIRMED 1835 VOTER with High confidence and identifies the 1840 household head as William Hanford Adams. This record restores that direct 1835 evidence to the canonical resident layer while leaving residence, occupation and family structure unasserted where the evidence does not support them. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Adams, William H., 451 Wabash avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Adams, W. H.” (poll_1833_001, line 22); Poll list of 1835 — “Adams, William H.” (poll_1835_001, line 286). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Adams' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: Issue #669 recovery. This is deliberately a one-person 1835 evidence container even though the linked 1840 census household contains two people. Five years of household change cannot be silently projected backward.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
